这次 OpenAI 开始亲自下场教大家怎么写 Skills 和 AGENTS. md 了，这篇最新 Blog 非常值得看。

一个很明显的信号是，模型变强以后，Agent Engineering 也得跟着升级。很多以前为了旧模型加上的规则，到了 Astra 这里可能已经成了负担。

几个实践建议我想可以直接抄：

Skill 尽量做窄，描述里重点写清楚「什么时候该调用」，复杂说明等真正用到时再加载。

AGENTS. md 少写那种一刀切的规则，比如「每次先读完整 Repo」「所有改动都跑全量测试」「任何不确定都先问人」。这些很容易让 Astra 过度搜索、过度验证。

同时把「什么算完成」「哪些事情可以自主决定」「什么时候需要人介入」提前讲清楚，反而更容易让它放开手干活。

我现在甚至觉得，每次换一代模型，都应该顺手给自己的 AGENTS. md 和 Skills 做一次大扫除。

模型升级了，之前给旧模型搭的脚手架也该拆一拆。

OpenAI 现在亲自开始讲这些，很推荐做 Coding Agent / Harness 的人看。

reviewedPosts.author: Xudong07452910
reviewedPosts.text:
一个 Agent 如果每次都要重新踩一遍坑，那它其实根本没学会工作。

Furong Huang 这篇讲的，就是 Agent 自进化里我觉得最关键的一件事：一次任务结束以后，经验有没有真的留下来，并改变下一次做事的方法。

比如 Coding Agent 第一次误改了 generated file，折腾半天才发现真正该改的是 generator。任务最后虽然成功，但如果一周后遇到类似问题，它还要重新踩一遍坑，那这次经验其实没真正留下来。

更理想的情况，是 Agent 把这次经历沉淀成新的工作方法。以后先判断文件是不是自动生成的、去哪里找源头、什么时候该重新生成，再根据后续任务继续修正这套流程。

所以这里的「学习」范围其实很大。

Memory、Skills、Tools、Workflow、Action Policy、Evaluator，甚至模型参数，都可以成为 Agent 自我改进的一部分。关键在于，过去的经验有没有真正改变它下一次做事的方式。

Skill 攒得多不代表真的进化，熟悉 Benchmark 上分更高也可能只是过拟合。更值得看的是，它面对之后的新任务时，能不能做得更准、更省 Token、更少需要人类救场。

再往后还有一个我很感兴趣的问题。

如果一个 Agent 已经踩过坑、学出了一套更好的方法，其他 Agent 能不能直接继承这份经验？

未来真正能 Scale 的，可能还有整个 Agent 系统「从干活中学习」的速度。

最近在关注 Agent 自进化的话，这篇很推荐。

https://t.co/dd3URhbYKi

reviewedPosts.author: fchollet
reviewedPosts.text:
I hope the proposals by frontier labs to pace AI research stem from a genuine concern for safety and a recognition of the potential risks posed by future models, rather than a strategic effort to consolidate power and permanently solidify the market dominance of a few top players.

If these efforts are genuine, then oversight must take a more democratic and accountable form, with both national and international components, similar to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in the US and the International Atomic Energy Agency internationally.

If there is only one organization responsible for safety monitoring, and it happens to be staffed by the same people as the frontier labs, and it is perfectly aligned with them both by incentives and by ideology, then it would be indistinguishable from letting frontier labs self-regulate and self-certify their own safety standards.

Two potential warning signs of regulatory capture to watch out for:

1. Calls to ban open-source AI. Open-source development currently serves as the only real counterweight to the dominance of frontier labs.

2. Attempts to hinder non-frontier research. Models that are one or two generations behind the frontier -- whose level of capability has already been deployed at scale -- are empirically known not to pose safety risks.

As long as we don't see 1 & 2, and we see real international coordination efforts, then I will optimistically believe that the proposals are benevolent.

reviewedPosts.author: sh_reya
reviewedPosts.text:
Lots of disdain in the comments. It’s honestly a bit unnerving to read people’s negative reaction to a harmless plea to continue prioritizing sharing discoveries and results, as humanity has done for millennia. Maybe it’s easy to think that the authors are operating from a place of ego and jealousy, if they are Fields medalists, and therefore the general public doesn’t trust them. So let me try explaining as someone who has no career achievements, no stake in the frontier labs, and no jealousy because my peers are all early-career like me 😆 

Academics are stewards of history. We have 3 jobs. (1) to train people / teach them what has been done in the past. (2) we make some discoveries ourselves, and (3) we regularly interact with our peers to learn about their discoveries; what tomorrow’s history may be. Many people think we just do (2), but in fact all 3 are important; otherwise we would be highly inefficient in problem-solving over the long term (centuries, millennia). 

We cannot really make AI the stewards of history (there are capitalist and geopolitical incentives not to). If we rid the world of academic values, there may not be immediate consequences, but things will be very bad in the long term. Progress will stall. Eventually folks will realize we need a clear and continually-updating ledger of history (ie “memory” for the AI-pilled folks). It will take a lot of work to rebuild this culture from first principles

On the optimistic side I think academics have a golden opportunity to figure out how we can harness AI in pursuit of our values. We can probably keep more information in our history, disseminate info more broadly, review and validate each others’ discoveries faster, etc. But, given that academics are powerless compared to these trillion dollar companies, we can only do the best we can—speak up; discuss; educate the public about academic values (which we haven’t really had to do since ww2); and, honestly, pray

This isn’t to say improving human lives isn’t important; it definitely is, but, i hope the people who use AI to make all these discoveries equally try to communicate what are the novel ideas—so we can apply them to other problems.

Proud of this statement from Dario on pacing - as anyone close to the technology knows, AI seems to be on a trajectory to progress far faster than the rate at which society can adapt to its capabilities and risks. AI is an amazingly positive technology - and an incredibly powerful one. For us to truly benefit from it we need to treat it seriously.

We need to find ways to slow the frontier of development, such that we can better deal with collective action problems and buy ourselves more time for understanding the properties of these systems and how they need to be handled.

On a personal note, as a parent of young children, it is an everyday crazymaking occurrence to reflect on how little the development of literal superintelligence is regulated relative to the food and toys I buy for my children.
